scenes.narration: Amazon is worth about two point nine three trillion dollars. That's two hundred and seventy dollars and eighty-seven cents a share at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six, times about ten point eight billion shares. And over the last twelve months, its free cash flow was minus forty-two billion dollars. Negative.

The cash didn't disappear. Amazon poured about two hundred and eleven billion dollars into capex, mostly data centers for A W S. And the bet behind it is a backlog. A W S says customers have committed about five hundred and seventy-eight billion dollars, up from about two hundred and forty-four billion dollars at the start of the year.
So what is this price actually betting on? What has to happen for all that spending to pay off? And what could break the story?

In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash into the data centers and the debt, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Amazon reports next.

Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Amazon's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself. And one disclosure. This episode was drafted with help from an A I made by Anthropic, a company that Amazon has invested in, and that appears in these filings.

scenes.narration: Over the last twelve months, Amazon sold about seven hundred and ninety-seven billion dollars worth of stuff and services. The stores in North America ran at an operating margin of about eight percent. International, about about three percent. Advertising brought in about seventy-eight billion dollars. But the profit engine is somewhere else.

It's A W S, the cloud. It made about one hundred and sixty-one billion dollars, only about twenty percent of sales, but about fifty-eight percent of all operating income, at a margin of about thirty-eight percent. And in the September quarter, A W S grew thirty-nine percent, its fastest growth in nearly five years.

The backlog is the headline. about five hundred and seventy-eight billion dollars of commitments, with an average remaining life of about six years. Two expansions are named in the filing. OpenAI added a hundred billion dollars over eight years, and Anthropic added more than a hundred billion over ten. Amazon doesn't say what share of the total they are.

Behind the stores there are quieter money streams too. Fees from outside sellers who use Amazon's marketplace and warehouses brought in about one hundred and eighty-eight billion dollars over the year. Advertising, about seventy-eight billion dollars. Prime and other subscriptions, about fifty-four billion dollars. And the cloud is speeding up, not slowing down. A W S growth went from twenty-four, to twenty-eight, to thirty-seven, to thirty-nine percent over the last four quarters, ignoring currency moves. One caution for the stores. Prime Day moved to an earlier quarter this year, which Amazon says cut the latest quarter's growth by about four percentage points.

scenes.narration: Operating cash flow over the last twelve months was about one hundred and sixty-eight billion dollars. Net income was about one hundred and thirty-five billion dollars, but about about seventy billion dollars of that came from marking up stakes, mostly in Anthropic, on paper. Capex took about two hundred and eleven billion dollars. So free cash flow came out at minus forty-two billion dollars.

To fill the gap, Amazon borrowed. Long-term debt went from about sixty-nine billion dollars at the end of last year to about one hundred and eighty-one billion dollars, in just nine months. And there are no buybacks and no dividend. The share count grew one point two percent in a year, from stock paid to employees.

Amazon also wrote big checks to A I labs. This year it put fifty billion dollars into OpenAI preferred stock and ten billion dollars into Anthropic. In total, its stakes and convertible investments are carried at about two hundred and ninety-nine billion dollars. Those labs are also among the A W S customers behind the backlog. Investor and supplier at the same time.

Put the balance sheet together and it has flipped. At the end of September, Amazon held about one hundred and fourteen billion dollars of cash and securities. It owed about one hundred and eighty-one billion dollars in long term debt, including a seventeen and a half billion dollars term loan taken in September. On top of that, lease liabilities add about ninety-nine billion dollars, and another about one hundred and sixty-five billion dollars of leases are signed but haven't started yet. That's the price of building data centers faster than the cash comes in.

And the company says the spending isn't done. It expects cash capex this year of approximately two hundred and twenty billion dollars, and it says capex will meaningfully increase again in twenty twenty-seven.

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the last twelve months. Price to earnings, about twenty-two times, but take out the paper gains and it's closer to about thirty-seven times. Free cash flow yield, below zero, so it tells us nothing. Operating cash flow yield, about five point seven percent.

So for a company in a building spree, we use a proxy. We take operating cash and subtract depreciation and amortization, about about seventy-nine billion dollars a year, as a rough stand-in for the spending needed just to keep things running. That leaves about eighty-nine billion dollars, a yield of about three percent. It's a proxy, and it assumes capex eventually falls back.

Now let's run it backwards. What growth in that cash, for ten years, makes today's price work, before slowing to three percent? With an eight percent discount rate, about nine percent a year. With ten percent, about fourteen percent. On actual free cash flow, the math doesn't even start, because it's negative.

So here's one more lens, our rough illustration. If Amazon were a steady business growing three percent a year from here, the price would need free cash flow of about about one hundred and forty-two billion dollars to about one hundred and ninety-nine billion dollars a year. Today it's minus forty-two billion dollars. That gap is the whole bet.

scenes.narration: Number one, the backlog converts. about five hundred and seventy-eight billion dollars of commitments has to turn into revenue over the next six years. The C E O says A W S is projected to grow over forty percent in both twenty twenty-seven and twenty twenty-eight. That's his projection, not ours.

Number two, A W S margins hold while depreciation ramps. The margin was close to thirty-nine percent last quarter. But depreciation and amortization is already about seventy-nine billion dollars a year, and every new data center adds to it.

Number three, the stores keep getting more profitable. Amazon guided fourth quarter operating income of between twenty-eight point five and thirty-three point five billion dollars, and sales between two hundred and forty and two hundred and forty-seven billion dollars. This year, operating income beat the top of its own range every single quarter.
And number four, capex peaks and free cash flow turns positive. Until then, the gap is filled with debt. The price needs that to change within a few years, not a decade.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one is the build-out itself. Amazon's own filing warns that misjudging demand can leave too much data center capacity and lead to impairment charges. It also says its A I investments may not earn enough to recoup the money. And it has about eight hundred and eighty-four billion dollars of commitments already signed.

Risk two is the loop. Amazon is an investor in the same A I labs that are big A W S customers. Their stakes are valued with models, and the filing admits private valuations are inherently complex. If those labs stumble, it hits the backlog and the stakes at the same time.

Risk three is regulators. In August, the F T C and twenty-two states sued over how Amazon prices its sponsored ad auctions. Older antitrust cases seek billions of dollars in damages. And last year's Prime settlement cost two point five billion dollars.

And then there's supply. Amazon says it relies on a limited group of suppliers for chips, including the graphics processors behind A I, and its own guidance flags supply swings in memory chips. A patent case at the International Trade Commission is seeking to block some A W S servers. And Amazon carries about about seven point three billion dollars of uncertain tax positions. None of these is sized as a loss, but each one could slow the build out.

And the upside the price might not fully include. The C E O says Amazon may have two trillion dollar revenue businesses in the next five to ten years. Its stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI are marked at about about two hundred and eighty-nine billion dollars. Those are marks and claims, not cash, so we won't count them as money in the bank.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected in early February twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, A W S growth and margin, and the backlog against about five hundred and seventy-eight billion dollars. Two, fourth quarter operating income against the guide. Three, capex and trailing free cash flow, now minus forty-two billion dollars, plus the outlook for twenty twenty-seven. If those hold up, the story the price is telling keeps holding up. If they crack, the debt gets much harder to defend.
That's Amazon, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
